channel.description: Latest articles from Cascade Policy Institute – Bias and Credibility (cascadepolicy.org)

item.title: A Trillion Dollar Energy Law - HB2021: Watch John Charles on PDX Real
item.description: In this special report, journalist Angela Todd breaks down Oregon’s House Bill 2021, explaining what the state’s Net Zero energy law requires, why electricity prices are rising, and what it could mean for Oregon’s energy future.

item.title: Testimony: SB 1526 Creates State-Sponsored Nonprofit for Net Zero Projects
item.description: Cascade Policy Institute President John Charles submitted testimony raising concerns about Oregon’s SB 1526, warning the bill could create a taxpayer-funded nonprofit to finance net-zero energy projects using public debt and environmental settlement funds. Charles urged lawmakers to conduct deeper review and postpone the proposal, citing duplication of existing programs and long-term financial risks for ratepayers and taxpayers.

item.title: Texas Parents Break Records for School Choice Applications
item.description: School choice is expanding rapidly across the United States, giving more than 1.5 million students access to alternative education options. With new programs launching in multiple states and record-breaking applications for Texas Education Freedom Accounts, families are gaining increased flexibility to choose learning environments that best fit their children’s needs. Expanding education choice programs aims to provide students with greater opportunities for success and personalized learning exp

item.title: Metro’s Plan for Making Housing More Expensive
item.description: Portland’s housing affordability crisis may be getting worse, not better. Critics argue Metro’s strategy of prioritizing high-density developments and subsidized housing is driving up costs, limiting single-family home options, and increasing taxpayer burdens. New analysis suggests expanding urban growth boundaries and allowing more housing choice could help restore affordability across the region.

item.title: Portland’s “Affordable” Housing Averages $800 per Square Foot
item.description: Taxpayer-funded “affordable housing” in Portland is costing far more than many private housing developments — sometimes three times as much per square foot. New data raises questions about efficiency, government spending, and whether these programs truly help lower housing costs. Read more about the numbers and what they could mean for Portland residents.

item.title: Will PPS Refuse to Comply with Federal Civil Rights Law?
item.description: The U.S. Department of Education has opened a civil rights investigation into Portland Public Schools over its Center for Black Student Excellence and race-based equity funding policies. The probe examines whether the district’s programs violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. With $70 million in federal funding potentially at stake, the controversy raises broader questions about equity, discrimination, and compliance with federal and state law.

item.title: Senate Bill 1511 on 20 Percent Death Tax Loses, Barely
item.description: Oregon lawmakers had a chance to reform the state’s estate tax—but instead considered making it even harsher. Critics say the proposal could push retirees, family wealth, and charitable giving out of the state. Now supporters are turning to Initiative Petition 51, which aims to end the Oregon estate tax and put the decision directly in voters’ hands in 2026.Should Oregon remain one of the few states with an estate tax, or is it time for voters to decide?

item.title: Report: “A Review of Metro’s Regional Passenger Rail Futures Study”
item.description: Metro’s study of Portland-area freight rail corridors reveals major challenges for turning them into passenger rail lines — including high operating costs, infrastructure needs, and limited ridership potential. Yet despite these findings, planners are still exploring ways to build demand and expand rail in the future. Should the region invest in preparing for passenger rail, or rethink its transportation priorities?

item.title: QuickPoint! Cascade’s Testimony on Metro Spending $50M, 40 Years, Turning Superfund Site to a Park
item.description: A 2012 Metro audit warned that expanding natural areas without a clear long-term maintenance plan could create major financial and management challenges. The case of Willamette Cove shows how acquiring former industrial land for parks can delay public access and burden taxpayers with decades of cleanup and stewardship costs.

item.title: Passenger Rail Wrong Fit for Portland, Metro Study Shows
item.description: Oregon lawmakers are being urged to take a closer look at Metro’s Regional Rail Futures Study. Despite findings showing high costs, infrastructure challenges, and limited ridership potential, regional rail is still on the table. Critics argue it’s time to rethink priorities—focusing on flexible, cost-effective bus networks that better reflect how people actually live and work across the Portland region today.
